description: We are Team Polaris from Dhaka, Bangladesh. For the Flame in Freefall challenge, we are engineering an AI dashboard to parse and compare NASA microgravity combustion experiments (PSI & BASS-II). Our goal is to extract verified flammability limits and material behaviors into grounded, citation-backed fire safety insights for spacecraft design.
summary:
FlameScope is an interactive research workspace that brings together NASA’s microgravity combustion data in one place, so researchers, students, and space enthusiasts can explore fire-safety questions for crewed habitats and see where evidence exists or is missing.

We developed a Mission Overview, a Test Explorer for NASA ACME, CFI, and SPICE gas and droplet experiments, a Compare view, and a Safety & Gaps page that highlights evidence-based findings and limited coverage. The “Will It Burn?” checker matches questions about solid cabin materials to individual test rows in NASA’s BASS-II report, showing outcomes, sources, or clear gaps. My Data Lab lets users overlay their own CSV data in the browser. VESTA, a tool-using AI assistant, helps users navigate evidence, run calculations, and generate charts, with a rules-based offline mode.

The challenge is that fire evidence is scattered across experiments, reports, and datasets. FlameScope unifies it and is transparent about what is not known: rankings are project-defined heuristics, not NASA ratings, and the data does not cover every material, atmosphere, or gravity level, including lunar and Martian gravity.

This matters because fire is one of the most serious risks on spacecraft, and understanding evidence gaps guides future research. FlameScope is an educational and research aid, not a safety certification.
details:
FlameScope: Will it burn in space? Ask NASA’s data.

Fire on a spacecraft doesn’t behave like fire on Earth. With no gravity, flames turn round, blue and sneaky. NASA has run hundreds of fire experiments on the ISS, but the results are buried in spreadsheets and technical reports. FlameScope digs them out and turns them into answers anyone can check.

What it does and how it works

  • 847 NASA fire tests (ACME, CFI, SPICE) plus 46 solid-material tests (BASS-II), cleaned and linked to their exact source row.
  • Will it burn? Ask “Will acrylic burn on the ISS?” and get Burned, 20 of 20 tests. Ask about a Moon base and get No data, because none of these tests ran at lunar gravity.
  • Mission check: Pick the ISS, a Moon base, a lunar rover or a spacesuit and see whether NASA ever tested that air.
  • VESTA, our AI crewmate: It uses 12 tools on the real data and answers with charts, sources and a confidence tag.

Benefits

  • Hours of report-reading become one question.
  • Every number is traceable to a NASA file. VESTA can’t make numbers up: a grounding check flags any number that isn’t in the data.
  • It works offline and free, with no paid AI key needed.

Intended impact

  • Artemis-era cabins may run on 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi, not the ISS’s 21% at 14.7 psi. FlameScope shows how much fire evidence carries over.
  • 518 tests are in range for ISS air, but only 28 for the lunar rover.
  • That gap tells engineers what to watch and tells researchers what to test next.

Tools we used

  • Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Three.js, ECharts, WebGL, Python (pandas, PyMuPDF)
  • Claude, Gemini, Groq and other AI engines, plus a no-AI Offline mode
  • A 353-test automated suite
  • Data from NASA PSI and NTRS
  • No hardware needed: it runs in any browser

what makes it creative

  • “No data” is a real answer, not a failure. Every gap becomes an experiment worth running.
  • A flame illustration that morphs with gravity, from Earth’s teardrop to the ISS’s blue ball.
  • A 3D habitat map of every NASA test, set between Earth and the Moon.

What we considered

  • Honesty first: no fake “safety scores” and no guessing beyond the data.
  • Open about limits: lunar and Martian gravity are untested, and only three solid materials have data.
  • Built for everyone: Student, Researcher and Engineer modes, on phones and desktops.

Built by Team Polaris, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
